doc_summary: Buck Shlegeris reports a pilot high-access red-team exercise (with METR) on OpenAI's internal agent misalignment monitoring, estimating monitoring coverage and finding vulnerabilities agents could exploit. He then derives design ideals for monitoring/control systems that withstand strategic, sustained attacks from capable internal agents.

items.claim: Prefers deep-access inspection of real infrastructure (code, configs, interviews) over black-box testing because it lets auditors quantify real coverage and find subversion paths that surface-level evals would miss.
items.quote: This exercise involved a deep level of access. The METR and Redwood employees had access to OpenAI’s internal codebase, misalignment-monitor prompts / configuration details, and internal documentation, and conducted technical interviews

items.claim: Prefers claims scoped explicitly to the system as it existed at a given time, with uncertainty stated, over broad claims about current safety because the system changed during the exercise and later fixes weren't verified.
items.quote: Our findings describe the historical system we assessed on and before July 21st, rather than the expanded system’s current coverage, which this exercise did not establish.

items.claim: Distinguishes identified-in-principle vulnerabilities from validated, exploited-in-practice ones, and flags when it did not validate or check actual exploitation.
items.quote: We did not validate this behavior or test whether it was exploitable in practice.

items.claim: Distrusts the developer's own reported claims and later patches without independent verification, and treats given statistics as suggestive rather than established.
items.quote: OpenAI has stated that all of the vulnerabilities we identified that impact their production safeguards stack have been patched. OpenAI has also described significant subsequent changes to the intended coverage of its monitoring system. We have not evaluated these claims.

items.claim: Prefers designing monitoring against deliberate, strategic, sustained attacks by highly capable internal agents over assuming benign or accidental failure because the threat model is adversarial agents at scale.
items.quote: we believe that future monitoring infrastructure should be able to withstand deliberate, strategic, and sustained attacks from highly capable internal agents at scale.

items.claim: Checks that the monitor sees the same context as the agent and cross-references logs of intended versus actual monitored traffic, since differences (serialization, compaction) create blind spots.
items.quote: periodically cross reference these logs with logs from the monitoring system directly to ensure everything that is intended to be monitored actually is. Maintain a list of all known ways around monitoring. Ensure that the monitor sees the same context as the agent.

items.claim: Looks for ways agents can influence whether or when monitoring runs (e.g., postponing by not returning control, setting headers), treating agent-controllable triggers as key attack surface.
items.quote: the monitoring system triggered when agents returned control to the user, so during the time period when compaction events were not being monitored, agents could indefinitely postpone being monitored by simply continuing to take actions.

items.claim: Prefers isolation between agents and their monitors, including withholding monitor design from agents, over relying on obscurity-free setups because agent knowledge and influence can enable subversion.
items.quote: Agents should not typically have access to the monitoring system design or code.

items.claim: Plans future versions of the exercise with better transparency and independence practices, and calls for ongoing control evaluations and methodology for evaluating strategic collusion.
items.quote: Periodically perform control evaluations, search for exploitable bugs in the monitoring system, and develop methodology to evaluate strategic collusion.
